title: Why Warnock Didn’t Sleep on Mississippi

A month later, C...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

“I am here because I am tired of the South being overlooked or diminished in terms of its electoral importance,” Senator Raphael Warnock told Mississippi Today back in October after stumping for Scott Colom. A month later, Colom won. He’s the first Black Mississippian elected to the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction. “We lose elections by the margins of our disengagement,” Warnock said then. “Mississippi is a blue state; it just doesn’t know it yet.”

Warnock, the pastor of Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church, was one of the few national Democrats who spent time in Mississippi this cycle. He raised hundreds of thousands of campaign dollars. Last week, when news outlets finally called the race in Mississippi, America woke up to the race everyone was “sleeping on,” as Warnock put it back in April.

Democrats, who had ceded the South to Republicans for the past several decades, now believe that the political possibilities in the region are changing and have even further to go; few Democrats on the national stage believe that as much as Warnock.

For this week’s episode of Radio Atlantic, I spoke with Warnock at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta about the uptick in turnout in the 2026 midterms, how to protect the vote in future elections, and what his agenda looks like in the years to come.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Senator Raphael Warnock: You have to compromise in politics. But I’m not going to compromise my integrity, just to maintain an office.

[Music]

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and today: a conversation with Senator Raphael Warnock about voting rights, the South, and what he wants to get done in the next Congress.

On January 5, 2021, Warnock became the first Black senator in Georgia’s history. A day later, rioters stormed the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C. And to Warnock, both events represent America. Those dates—January 5 and January 6—represent the promise and the violence of its history

And to him, when Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi’s Senate race, Warnock believed it was another promising moment. Few people – including national Democrats – believed Colom’s win was possible, but Warnock did. He was one of the few who supported him early and often.

He says it’s because he believes a new South is a real possibility.

On Thursday evening, at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, I sat down with Senator Warnock to talk about what needs to be done to protect voting rights, what political success looks like for Democrats, and how to hold the tension that America is both January 5 and January 6.

Here’s our conversation:

Adam Harris: Senator, it’s great to be with you this evening.

Raphael Warnock: It’s great to be home. I just landed a few minutes ago. I came straight here. Didn’t pass go, didn’t collect $200.

Harris: I love it.

Warnock: Good to see everybody.

Harris: Yeah, absolutely, and thank you all for joining us. I’ve been looking forward to this conversation, particularly as we’ve seen the South change a bit over the last couple of days. For a long time, political possibility in the South has been sort of limited by both discrimination and also sort of lack of imagination.

In 2021, you became Georgia’s first Black senator. What does Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi, what do these wins in Georgia tell us about political possibility in the South?

Warnock: What a remarkable moment in American history. And I’m just honored and deeply humbled to be a small part of it. I’m so happy for the people of Mississippi.

But let’s be clear: Mississippi did an incredible thing for the whole country. The country is better. They nudged us a little closer to our ideals. And Scott Colom ran an incredibly innovative, creative, and scrappy campaign because he had very little resources. People didn’t believe.

But I wanna be clear, because sometimes on the other side of these victories, we forget what it costs. This didn’t roll in on the wheels of inevitability. I know what it’s like for people to believe, for people to think you can’t do it. And it always looks impossible until it’s done. That’s where we were here in Georgia. Cycle after cycle, we kept telling folks, It can happen in Georgia, and they didn’t believe us.

Harris: You just invest.

Warnock: And we kept falling short. Don’t forget that. Because it’s easy to forget now that I’m here. And the great Jon Ossoff is here. A Black senator and a Jewish senator in one fell swoop. Right? But representing the whole state. But I don’t want you to miss this: The people of Mississippi did an amazing thing. I know you were wondering, Well, when are they gonna finish counting all those ballots?

But here’s the question you ought to ask yourself: Why is that the case?

So there were provisional ballots, and why were there provisional ballots? Because people had been purged from the roll. Georgia, by the way, was quite good at that. They purged 500,000 voters one Saturday night here in Georgia.

And so people’s names had been purged from the rolls, and so that’s why they had to cast a provisional ballot. And they had to vote on Election Day—only on Tuesday, because you don’t vote early in Mississippi without an excuse.

So think about that. Why do you need an excuse to vote? So early voting is virtually nonexistent. You’ve got these rural communities where it’s not necessarily easy to get to the polls. It’s a poll tax on working people because the only time you can vote is on Tuesday during work hours. And somehow those folks overcame all of those barriers just to be able to exercise the franchise, which is not a privilege. Don’t ever say voting is a privilege. It’s not a privilege; it’s a right. It’s a right. Driving is a privilege. Voting is a right. And they overcame all of that, and here we are.

Harris: And actually, to that point, speaking of the things that they overcame: One of the stories of this cycle was the turnout. Here in Georgia, you had 160,000 more Black folks cast ballots than cast ballots in 2022, right? But over the last two decades, we’ve seen voting protections weakened, right? This was done in spite of all of the ways that the franchise has been limited.

And because voting is so foundational, as they said in 1886—the Supreme Court said that it was protective of all other rights, that voting was foundational to democracy. What does strengthening that right to vote look like?

Warnock: Well, it’s job one, and I spend a lot of time working on voting rights and strengthening our democracy. Because voting rights is not just one other issue alongside other issues. This radical idea that no matter your income, no matter your race, no matter who you are, you get to vote and your vote gets to count—that’s the framework in which we get to fight, so we have to always preserve that.

And we have witnessed the erosion of those fundamental rights over the last few years. And so it’s important that you help your neighbors who say, “What do you mean? Everybody can vote.” You’re right. So the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendment were passed following slavery, part of the work of Reconstruction.

So I want you to remember that Black people had a right to vote, at least on paper, for 100 years before the voting-rights law was passed. So just because it’s on paper, that doesn’t mean there aren’t real barriers. And Mississippi embodies that, but it’s not alone.

So we have seen the erosion of voting rights over the last several years. That is part of the ugly legacy, in my view, of the Roberts Court, Shelby v. Holder, which said that the states that had previously been under what’s known as “preclearance”—We’re way past that. Why are we still doing that? And they removed those protections. Ruth Bader Ginsburg, bless her memory, when she wrote her dissenting opinion to that decision, she said, “We’re removing our umbrella in the middle of a rainstorm because we’re not getting wet.” And her words proved to be tragically correct.

I don’t want it to get lost on you that in spite of these incredible turnouts that we’re seeing and the incredible results we saw last Tuesday in response to this attack on voting rights—in response to Callais, right? Which added fuel to partisan gerrymandering—Black and brown voters alongside white sisters and brothers created a coalition of conscience, responded in response to this. But it shouldn’t be lost that in the years since Shelby v. Holder, the racial voter-turnout gap has widened. And it’s widened twice as fast in the states that used to be under preclearance. The very states that have a history of discrimination, and so they’re under Section 5—which says that if you’re gonna make some changes, you gotta run it by the Justice Department—that gap has increased twice as fast in those states.

So you’ve got Shelby v. Holder. You’ve got Citizens United, which is a scourge on our democracy. It’s diminishing the voices of ordinary people while raising the voices of corporate, wealthy, and well-connected entities. And then you had Callais in which the Supreme Court was deeply intellectually dishonest when it said you can’t have minority opportunity districts because that’s reverse racism, while leaving partisan gerrymandering intact. And we know that especially in the South, you can’t neatly disaggregate partisan gerrymandering from racial gerrymandering.

I think race was the reason why we had it in the first place. And so we literally saw these states gerrymandering the districts while folks were voting.

And so what happened last Tuesday is the American people stood up and said, Enough. They were upset about this. They’re crushed by these terrible gas prices, the price of groceries. And they stood up to take back their democracy. For me, I take it as a sacred trust. And I feel deeply obligated to try to deliver for the people who gave us a chance to fight for them.

Harris: And when you think about that, delivering for the folks who fought, right? You argue in the book that looks like the John Lewis voting-rights—

Warnock: What book are you talking about? Hold it up.

(Audience laughs.)

Listen, I got a 10-year-old and a 7-year-old. I have college tuition to pay. You know, the Senate has been a place where the aristocracy has sent its sons, and then daughters. That is not my story. The Crooked Places Made Straight: Reflections on the Moral Meaning of America.

Harris: So in the first couple chapters of the book, you focus on voting. You mentioned Citizens United. This was the most expensive midterm race in history: $12 billion spent in this midterm cycle. And that number seems to grow with every election. How do we begin to wean off of money in politics?

Warnock: It’s insane, when I think about what it cost for me to win this Senate seat. Because all of us are part of that system. I’m embarrassed how much money it took for me to win this seat, but at the same time, I know I can’t unilaterally disarm. I wouldn’t be here.

But Citizens United—one of the most important things we can do for our democracy is to get dark money out of our system, and to create a system where billionaires spend a whole lot less on elections and a whole lot more in taxes.

The American people sense in their gut—because they’re smart; they get it—that the system is rigged. And they’re right. They’re not wrong about that. It’s rigged. But we’ve seen increasing wealth inequality in this country since Citizens United. That’s not an accident. The wealthy, the well-connected, the top 1 percent or so of the country that’s got more money than the bottom 53 percent, they like it like this. And that wealth inequality is greater than it was during the Gilded Age. And, so for me, it’s a democracy question. I want people to have a voice in the direction of their country and their place within it, which is why we’ve gotta pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act (Audience applauds.) which would deal with dark money in our politics. We need to reverse Citizens United, even if we have to do it by a constitutional amendment. (Audience applauds.) We need to get rid of partisan gerrymandering (Audience applauds.) in our politics. Gerrymandering is turning the democracy on its head so that rather than the people picking their representatives, gerrymandering is the politicians cherry-picking their voters. So we need to deal with partisan gerrymandering, and we need to make sure that the so-called SAVE Act never sees the light of day.

Harris: Do you think any of those legislative actions are possible in this next Congress? It’ll be a lame-duck session. But do you think any of that is possible in this Congress?

Warnock: Well, one of the things—so I’d like to pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act because it’ll address a lot of these things that I’m talking about. But in the meantime, I would like to offer in the new Congress a slender and skinny bill to deal with gerrymandering. And I have that bill. I’m gonna offer that bill in the Congress. We ought to deal with gerrymandering.

I’m a Democrat, but I’m an American first. And I think it’s bad for the democracy that there are so few truly competitive congressional districts in our country. And so folks got busy after Callais last spring, gerrymandering these districts a few months before the election. Well, as we say in church, God works in mysterious ways.

And maybe, maybe after some of my Republican friends got crushed in their own gerrymandered districts, there might be some takers who will join me in this effort to get rid of gerrymandering altogether.

[Break]

Harris: You talk about that hope in your book, The Crooked Places Made Straight.

Warnock: There it is.

(Audience laughs.)

Harris: (Laughs.) In your book, you look at politics through a moral lens, through a Christian lens. You talk about where your hope comes from, sort of through the Book of Isaiah in particular. And it’s easy to get cynical about politics. At one point, you wrote about the ways that your congregation at Ebenezer was worried that politics would make their pastor sort of lose his prophetic voice, that it would sort of change you. Can you talk about how your faith informs your politics, and how you can keep it central through the cynicism of the political arena?

Warnock: I am not a senator who used to be a pastor. I’m a pastor who serves in the Senate, and my faith is what got me in this mess in the first place, called politics. I have a faith that seriously believes that faith ought to live in the messiness and complexity of everyday life.

I’ve never wanted a stained-glass-window faith that’s encased in a museum, and you bump into it on Sunday morning, and then you walk out, and then you pick it back up on Sunday. My faith lives in the public square. Always has. Long before I served in the Senate, long before I knew I would even run. My whole career, I’ve been at Ebenezer now 21 years, and I pastored for many years before that. I’ve always been an activist pastor. I was fighting for health care before I was your senator. I was trying to get Georgia to expand Medicaid way back in 2014, when the ACA was passed. I was trying to get our state to expand Medicaid.

What drives me to your question is: I remain rooted in my faith. I return to my pulpit every Sunday morning. I still serve as pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, and folks ask me, “Why do you do that? Because you’re pretty busy as a senator.” Well, I return to my church, and I continue to lead that church, because I don’t wanna spend all my time talking to politicians. I’m afraid I might accidentally become one. I wanna be a public servant who’s in politics. You have to compromise in politics. But I’m not going to compromise my integrity, just to maintain an office.

I’m grateful for this set of tools for the period of time that I have it, and whenever that changes, I’ll have another set of tools. But the mission is the same: human liberation; human thriving; building a country where every child has a chance, where a child’s outcome is not based on their parents’ income, where people have access to health care and affordable housing and the dignity that comes with that.

Harris: You wrote in the book, “We all share a basic human longing for purpose and connection that transcends our narrow self-interest.” And that struck me, particularly given that there are folks who call themselves Christian at the moment who argue that empathy is something that their flocks should look away from.

Can you talk about that idea that we share that longing for things beyond ourselves, when you have examples of folks who do not?

Warnock: So one of the things that is unfortunate and keeps me up at night is the recognition that some of the meanest and most hateful voices in our country are Christian voices.

The data shows that evangelical Christians—again, not all—but the data shows that evangelical Christians are more likely than any other group to blame the poor for their poverty, to somehow surmise that their material deficiency is somehow reflective of a moral deficiency.

And so I want you to think about that. Like, what is it about our theology, what’s being preached on Sunday morning that causes people to blame poor people for being poor, and to moralize about that and not see this wealth inequality that I’m talking about, the fact that people work and they don’t have a livable wage.

To me, when I see this mean-spirited Jesus, I don’t know who they’re talking about. The Jesus that whom I preach on Sunday morning—I’m a Matthew 25 Christian. Said, “I was hungry and you fed me. I was thirsty; you gave me something to drink. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison; you came to see about me. I was a stranger, an immigrant, and you welcomed me.” And they asked Jesus, “When were you hungry? When were you thirsty? When were you sick? When were you a prisoner? When were you an immigrant?” He said, “Inasmuch as you’ve done it unto the least of these, you’ve done it also unto me.”

And so that’s my faith. I don’t know how anyone gets this idea that empathy somehow is anathema. Empathy is not only central to Christian faith; empathy is central to all of the great faith traditions. I think empathy is the first step of good public policy and good politics.

If you can’t see your neighbor, how are you going to represent your neighbor?

Harris: We’ve discussed voting. Where do you see other opportunities for action, for policy, change?

Warnock: Well, the great thing is that the American people stood up, and they spoke very clearly. And they are sick and tired of this lawless war of choice that is making us less safe and driving up gas prices, the price of diesel. And when you drive up the price of diesel, because almost everything you got—everything you have arrived on a truck—so it’s raising the price of everything. They’re weary of these tariffs, which is a tax, a sales tax on everything you buy, and they want us to fix health care. So that’s what I wanna do. I wanna end the war. I wanna stop these tariffs. I wanna pass these premium tax credits so that people’s health-care premiums aren’t twice as much next year as they are now—triple, quadruple in some cases. And then once we stop the bleeding, I think we need to lay out a bold vision for our country.

I still think we can do big things. And I’m not convinced that we suffer from a poverty of resources. We suffer from a poverty of moral imagination and moral courage. And so I’m ready to roll up my sleeves and work alongside all of my colleagues, Democrats and Republicans, and move the country forward.

Harris: We’ve seen some of the ways that Republicans have sort of doubled down on the policy of the first two years of this administration, though, promoting Stephen Miller to become the chief of staff. Jim Jordan will be the House minority leader. What do you make of that doubling down? Is there space to work with the president? Do you think that the administration will be—

Warnock: Listen, we have to do what the American people asked us to do. And we have to fight for this with or without our Republican colleagues. But we need some guardrails on this president. That’s a good first start. We literally witnessed a Congress that went along with everything he did. Watching the last two years, you wouldn’t know that tariffs are in the purview and authority of Congress. I know you forgot because the Congress isn’t asserting its authority.

What we’ve witnessed in tragic fashion is what happens if one branch voluntarily just hands over its power. I’ll tell you what happens: You get Pete Hegseth as the secretary of defense; and you get Robert F. Kennedy as the secretary of health and human services, and all of a sudden you’re dealing with measles, again. Measles? Really?

Harris: Measles.

Warnock: It means that you’ve got tariffs on just about everything, and people are crushed. And thankfully, the American people, even in ruby-red districts who’ve been suffocating in this economy, said, Enough. And so we’ve got some guardrails on this president. When you get a result that you don’t want in an election, what you’re supposed to do is course-correct. Don’t start playing with the lines. What you’re supposed to do is course-correct. So hopefully with such a clear message, we can find some common ground to do things that the American people want us to do.

Harris: You wrote that “America is both January 5 and January 6. It has always contained both of those elements throughout its history.” If this election is a January 5, how do we prevent the next January 6?

Warnock: That’s a great question. On January 5, 2021, the people of Georgia did an amazing thing: They sent a kid who grew up in public housing—Cayton Homes Housing Project, Savannah, Georgia. First college graduate in my family, number 11 out of 12. My folks read the scriptures, “Be fruitful and multiply.” (Audience laughs.) They sent this Black kid who grew up in the projects alongside a Jewish kid who was the son of an immigrant—both of us touched in different ways by John Lewis—to the United States Senate in one fell swoop, at a moment when we’re all suffocating under the thick air of COVID and the bigotry unleashed in the Trump years.

And I was feeling great the next morning. I was like, Oh, I’ve arrived. I was on Morning Joe. I was on Good Morning America. I was on The View talking to Whoopi Goldberg. (Audience laughs.) I had arrived. I was feeling really good about myself. That was the morning of January 6. And by lunchtime, we all know what happened.

That other side of our grand American experiment reared its ugly head. And so January 5 is who we are, where a Black kid and a Jewish kid can be United States senators from Georgia. What we must hold in tension is the recognition that we’re both of those things. Both January 5 and January 6 tell us something important about who America is, and it’s too easy to say we’re one and not the other.

When January 6 happened, people kept saying, This is not who we are. And I understand the sentiment that they were trying to express, but it’s not true. January 6 is who we are; it’s who we’ve always been. It’s a part of who we are, and when we’re in denial about that, we can’t fix it.

The good news is that that’s not all that we are. We don’t have to ban books. We don’t have to lie about our history. We don’t have to pretend like our children are so tender and so fragile that we have to lie to them and call slavery a jobs program.

I had an older father who was a World War II–era veteran. And it’s a blessing to have had an older father. There’s a wisdom that comes with that. And he used to tell us the story about how one day, while dressed in his soldier’s uniform, he had to give up his seat on the bus to a white teenager. He’s dressed in his soldier’s uniform, preparing to make the world safe for democracy. My old man is asked to give up his bus seat to a teenager because the skin he was wearing was apparently more important than the uniform he was wearing.

And decades later, the man who had to give up his bus seat has a son who sits in a Senate seat. We’re both of those things. And what I love about the country is that we get to keep fighting for what’s the better part of that story. Because we don’t need to “make America great again.” This is a great country, and we’re just trying to push it a little bit closer to its ideals because it can be greater yet.

(Audience applauds.)

Harris: Thank you so much. We’ll have to leave it there.

[Music]

This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Eibed is the executive producer of Podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues here at The Atlantic you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
summary: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face lega...
content:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

title: The Dangerous Idea Rubio and Hegseth Are Endorsing
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.When Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was reprimanded by a sentinel last week for a lack of decorum at...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

When Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was reprimanded by a sentinel last week for a lack of decorum at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, his response was unusually gracious: He promptly awarded the sentinel the Joint Service Commendation Medal. Perhaps Hegseth’s conciliatory response was not because he recognized he’d violated the sanctity of the location, but because he’d been yelled at by one authority he recognizes: a man with a gun.

This thought occurred to me over the weekend, when Hegseth posted a clip of Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaking at a Federalist Society conference Friday evening. Rubio praised President Trump’s sanctions earlier this year on the International Criminal Court. So far, so normal: The right has long despised the ICC, arguing that it violates American sovereignty and could be used as a foreign-policy weapon by U.S. adversaries. Then things got strange. Rubio said that if the ICC tried to exercise jurisdiction over Americans, “our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general, Pompey, when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

This is an odd thing to say to a room full of lawyers, and it was met with some awkward chuckles. Only once Rubio declared Pompey’s statement as “not politically correct” did he win applause. But Hegseth was apparently taken with the quote and reposted it, writing, “Stop quoting laws to MEN WITH SWORDS.”

Rubio and Hegseth are expressing a core view of the second Trump administration: that might makes right and rules are for sissies. In January, now–White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller explained the American quasi-colonization of Venezuela this way. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world,” he said, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.” (No wonder that the United States—with Rubio acting as viceroy—has signaled that it prefers rule by the Nicolás Maduro protégé Delcy Rodríguez to María Corina Machado’s attempts to restore democracy in the country.) Trump has shown that he prefers the performative machismo of Vladimir Putin’s Russian military to Ukraine’s legal and moral claim on its land, and he has mused publicly about actions against Iran that would be war crimes.

The Trumpist fidelity to this idea is particularly true with regard to international law, but it extends to a consistent disregard for the laws of the United States as well. At the Pentagon, Hegseth has raged against rules of engagement for the military and loosened them for the war in Iran, which may be one reason that the U.S. bombed an elementary school in Iran early in the conflict. (Superior American military might has not prevailed in Iran so far, either.) The military has also killed almost 250 people in extrajudicial and likely illegal strikes on boats that American officials allege are carrying drugs.

The epithet un-American is overused, but in this case, it is literally true. “The very purpose of the American founding was to ensure that force would always be subject to law, which would itself flow from natural right and popular consent,” John R. Puri writes in National Review. “That is why one of the Founders’ great innovations was to place the new U.S. armed forces under strict civilian control.” One specific complaint in the Declaration of Independence was that King George III had “affected to render the Military independent of and superior to the Civil power.” By contrast, John Adams wrote that a republic was a government “of Laws, and not of Men,” a stipulation that very much includes men with swords who might try to supersede law.

Hegseth is himself now a lawless man with (metaphorical) swords, and in his enthusiastic endorsement of Rubio’s remark, we may find insight into both why Hegseth joined the Army out of college and why his career languished. Maybe he thought joining the military was a ticket to cracking heads without restriction. Instead, he found a careful, disciplined, and rule-abiding force, and he never advanced very far. As my colleague Eliot A. Cohen has written, “The Army, unlike Princeton and Harvard, knew a petulant, insecure mediocrity when it saw one.” Hegseth eventually left the National Guard when he was sidelined over concerns about extremism. As secretary, he has gone about destroying the institution that spurned him, as well as working to ensure that the people bearing swords are almost entirely men.

As for Rubio, he has recently become a fount of classical references, perhaps under the influence of white-nationalist ideas circulating at the State Department. But mouthing these words is different from understanding what they mean. As a young commander during a Roman civil war in the 80s B.C.E., Pompey earned the nickname adulescentulus carnifex—“teenage butcher.” When residents of the Sicilian city of Messana resisted his authority, citing ancient Roman law, he uttered the quotation that Rubio cites. The American Founders—and indeed most Americans throughout history—would have seen themselves in the citizens of Messana, not the ruthless general.

Things didn’t turn out well for Pompey. He enjoyed years of political and military success during a period when republican rule was teetering, eventually becoming part of a ruling triumvirate with Julius Caesar and Marcus Licinius Crassus. But he eventually fell out with Caesar, resulting in another civil war. Pompey fled Rome but was killed and beheaded in Egypt. Nor, more important, did Pompey’s era end well for the Roman Republic. When the long-running political crisis that spawned both civil wars was over, the republic was dead, and Rome was ruled by an emperor.

It is possible—even probable—that the Trump figures quoting Pompey do not know this history. But understanding it is not necessary to grasp why Pompey’s words are nothing to emulate, nor to predict what will happen to a republic that allows such leaders to reach and maintain power.

Awesome

By Adrienne LaFrance

In Jules Verne’s wildest imagination, the technology that would send humanity starward was already familiar on Earth. The launching mechanism for the American rocket, in Verne’s 1865 novel From the Earth to the Moon, is—of all things—a colossal cannon. The speed required to reach the lunar surface, he reasoned, would require a gunshot of a launch. So in Vernian terms, a starship was not merely launched but “fired” into space.

I’ve been thinking of Verne today as I watched the video (then watched it again, and again) of SpaceX’s latest history-making maneuver. Yesterday, for the first time ever, engineers successfully pulled off a midair landing—using the company’s Mechazilla tower’s “chopstick” arms to snatch a starship the size of a skyscraper out of the sky after it had spent the past 22 hours in Earth’s orbit. Up until this point, Mechazilla’s chopsticks had caught boosters after launch—that is, the part of the rocket that detaches—but never ships themselves.

title: The Real Reason Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond
summary: Picking a new James Bond has long followed a tried-and-tested formula: Don’t go too famous. The secret agent has nearly always been played by an up-and-coming, well-regarded talent who looks good in a tux. So for years, as the debate has dragged on over who would replace Daniel Craig in the role, do...
content:
Picking a new James Bond has long followed a tried-and-tested formula: Don’t go too famous. The secret agent has nearly always been played by an up-and-coming, well-regarded talent who looks good in a tux. So for years, as the debate has dragged on over who would replace Daniel Craig in the role, dozens of names along those lines have bubbled up; these most recently included Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor. Some possible candidates aged out of the role while waiting for it to open up, in the same way that potential popes find themselves hitting retirement age before their chance at the papacy arrives. But the final choice for the new Bond, Robert Pattinson, completely defies that established logic: By casting someone who’s already globally popular, the franchise is somehow taking the risky version of a typically very safe bet.

Pattinson makes plenty of sense on paper as Bond: He’s about the right age (he turned 40 this year) and the right height, at 6 foot 1; he’s debonair and British in all the appreciable ways; he wears a suit better than anyone. (His work in Tenet is one of the best-tailored performances of all time.) But unlike most of his predecessors, he’s also one of the most famous A-listers working today. He’s featured in multiple hit franchises and is also the current occupant of another iconic role, Batman. And because the Bond franchise is in the hands of new ownership for the first time in decades, the old formulas clearly no longer apply.

Pattinson’s career started out traditionally enough. He first broke out as a teenager playing Cedric Diggory in the fourth Harry Potter movie before becoming a superstar in his 20s thanks to the Twilight movies—dark romantic fantasies aimed at young adults that were largely dismissed or mocked by critics upon release. But the actor has harnessed his early celebrity to create a constantly shifting and unique persona as a performer. He’s worked with numerous acclaimed directors across genres, Christopher Nolan, David Cronenberg, James Gray, Claire Denis, the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers, Bong Joon Ho, and Lynne Ramsay among them. When he’s appeared in more conventional blockbusters, he’s put a weird imprimatur on them, as with his emo version of Batman; in December, he’s popping up in Dune: Part Three as an eyebrow-less, shapeshifting villain.

[Read: The James Bond trap]

In a way, playing Bond seems almost too normal for Pattinson. He certainly looks the part in the one promo image that Amazon dropped; he’s a handsome Brit with a chiseled jaw who’s clad in a tux and toting a gun, as per usual for the MI6 super-spy. But one hopes he’ll be able to bring a stranger energy to the role than the Bonds before him. Craig played the character in five movies, culminating in 2021’s No Time to Die; his take was flinty and frightening, a swerve from Pierce Brosnan’s suave demeanor. Pattinson will likely come across as even more sophisticated—he’s taller and more willowy than Craig, and more traditionally “posh.” And the DC cinematic universe’s recent behind-the-scenes shake-up probably helped Pattinson commit to the franchise, considering that his future as Batman now seems murky. But I hope there’s room in his schedule to maintain the wacky streak he’s shown in movies such as last year’s Mickey 17, as well as the more alien, lizard-like quality that made his performance in The Batman, along with this year’s The Odyssey and Primetime, so compelling.

In previous eras, one would be foolish to hope for that sort of originality. The Bond property had long been a rarity in Hollywood: It was essentially run as a tightly controlled family business. Eon Productions, which was led by the producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli, managed the franchise that they’d inherited from their father; creatively, the buck stopped with them. They relied on a core group of collaborators who knew what a Bond movie should look and feel like, extending beyond whoever was playing the role. That consistency was helpful in building the brand, but it sometimes felt stultifying. Now that Amazon owns Bond outright, the company is making choices that suggest that a more prestigious take on the character is en route.

This is not to diss some of the prior Bond films’ directors. Sam Mendes, who made two of the Craig movies, is an Oscar winner—yet he’d made a few flops before he got the gig. Directors such as Cary Fukunaga, Marc Forster, Martin Campbell, and Lee Tamahori were all fairly reliable picks with some large-canvas action experience. But the next installment’s director, Denis Villeneuve, is a glitzy choice: He’s highly regarded by critics and is coming off a giant franchise success of his own with Dune. Among action filmmakers, only Nolan is a bigger name right now (and he was reportedly counted out for the job because he’d require the right to final cut—i.e., total creative control).

Amazon’s decision to spare no expense or risk for handling the biggest name-brand property it owns seems obvious. For all the creative ups and downs of the Craig era, the actor was a beloved Bond for 15 years; his memory will be difficult to displace. Rather than roll the dice on a (relative) unknown in search of something new and different, the brand’s new owners are opting for A-list quality. Pattinson is not an outside-the-box choice for Bond. Somehow, he still feels like a total surprise.

title: Sorry, Robert Pattinson Is Not James Bond
summary: Robert Pattinson is, I’m sure, a fine actor. I cannot vouch for this because I have not seen him in movies I’ve liked. Granted, I have not seen his entire body of work; I was already in my 40s when he landed his big role as a vampire in Twilight, a movie that was not exactly aimed at my demographic....
content:
Robert Pattinson is, I’m sure, a fine actor. I cannot vouch for this because I have not seen him in movies I’ve liked. Granted, I have not seen his entire body of work; I was already in my 40s when he landed his big role as a vampire in Twilight, a movie that was not exactly aimed at my demographic. I am a fan of superhero movies, and he was, in my view, a terrible Batman: He made Bruce Wayne into a dull cop in a costume. Still, he seems to be working a lot, so someone out there likes him.

But is he James Bond? No. Amazon MGM Studios, which now owns the movie franchise, announced today that he’ll take over the role. Yet Pattinson lacks the manly gravitas, the physicality, the wit, to play the world’s most dangerous spy.

I’m a Bond superfan. As a kid, I saw the Sean Connery movies only on television. I was 13 when I saw my first Bond film on a big screen: Live and Let Die, starring Roger Moore. It was a revelation. (I was old enough to start getting the jokes about sex, for one thing.) I then devoured, in proper sequence, all the Ian Fleming novels that inspired the movies. When I visited London as a teen in 1975, I didn’t care about seeing Parliament or the crown jewels. I wanted to be Moore—hey, he was the only movie Bond working at the time—and wander the streets once walked by the British spy who always saved the world and got the girl.

I know the voice, mannerisms, and quips of every cinematic Bond. I also know what Fleming’s Bond looks and sounds like. According to Fleming, he was based on the 1940s bandleader Hoagy Carmichael, if that makes any sense to you, and I even know where Bond’s boss, M, has his office and his favorite club. (I also know his full name: Miles Messervy. You’re welcome.) I know what Bond’s maid, May, makes him every day for breakfast.

In other words, I know James Bond. James Bond is a friend of mine. And Robert Pattinson, you are no James Bond.

[From the March 2024 issue: The James Bond trap]

Bond does not need to be a hairy bruiser; in the movies he loses plenty of fights, and in the books he routinely gets beaten to a pulp and ends up in the enemy’s clutches. Connery was perhaps the most macho of the Bonds, whereas Moore was the most dainty. All of them, however, were charismatic rogues, mature adults who could shoot, fight, drink, and—well, other things. They enjoyed every martini and they made a play for every shapely woman who crossed their path. (Bond is suave and a hero, but he’s also a boozy, sexist boor.)

Can Pattinson carry the legacy of any of his predecessors? Aficionados will disagree on who made the best Bond, but each actor had a niche. Connery was a product of the Cold War and the swinging ’60s. (He came back to play Bond once in 1971, Diamonds Are Forever, a misfire that included fitting him with a bad toupee; he made one more mediocre Bond film in 1983 with a different production company as a one-off outside the “canonical” Bond series.) A temporary replacement Bond, an Australian named George Lazenby, did a fine job in one movie, and then blew his career by walking away from the character. Moore, like the rest of us, did his best to make his way through the silly 1970s, but I think he is underappreciated: His 007 grimly faced down Christopher Lee in The Man With the Golden Gun and dispatched not one but two genocidal freaks bent on planetary destruction: a web-fingered weirdo in The Spy Who Loved Me and a eugenics-obsessed, space-industry billionaire—a plot clearly ahead of its time—in Moonraker.

Moore was a decent Bond, but stayed with the role too long. In 1985, the 57-year-old Moore had a love scene with 36-year-old Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. Let us not speak of it again.

Timothy Dalton, another underappreciated Bond, was an accomplished Shakespearean actor who moved into the role easily, and brought a combination of Connery’s violent physicality and Moore’s caddish humor. (Watch the pre-credits sequence of The Living Daylights, which is one of the best cold opens in the entire series.) Producers had begun looking at the next Bond, Pierce Brosnan, when he was still playing the TV detective Remington Steele and was too young and callow to play a spy who was licensed to kill. But as he matured, he was an obvious choice to play Bond perhaps like no actor since Connery. Brosnan took Bond into the new, post–Cold War world with style, but also with murderous determination: In GoldenEye, one of the best Bond movies, Brosnan looks directly into his best friend’s face and then drops him to his death.

All of these men as Bond exuded a kind of energetic and masculine combination of professionalism and uncontrollable individuality. In the books, 007 is a complex character who soldiers on because it’s his job. He is sometimes morose and regretful. But all of that anguish would make for a drab series of movies, and to their credit, Connery, Lazenby, Moore, Brosnan, and even the dour Dalton manage to look they’re having fun—at least when they’re not about to be cut in half by lasers or strangled by a python.

Here I will aggravate a lot of Bond fans: I think the series went off the rails with the casting of Daniel Craig and a drastic change in the 007 scripts. Instead of taking on supervillains, Bond tussled with terrorists and financiers, all while thinking and talking way too much about his psyche. Craig, another fine actor, was too brutish, and the scripts make plain that the job did, in fact, get to him. Craig’s Bond dressed well enough, but he always seemed uncomfortable in his suits: He’s a brawler with deep, complicated feelings, and one thing the cinematic James Bond does not need is a lot of feelings. The Craig scripts became like therapy sessions: When the big reveal came in the Craig movie Spectre—that the sadistic, megalomaniacal genius Ernst Blofeld was actually just a little boy with hurt feelings whose dad liked Jimmy Bond better when they were kids—I nearly walked out of the theater. (And by the way, what an utter waste of Christoph Waltz, who was born to play Blofeld.)

By settling on Pattinson, who is even more angsty than Craig, the producers seem intent on continuing the decline. At least in the performances I’ve seen, Pattinson is sensitive; he broods; he’s conflicted; he has messy hair; he has deep, watery eyes; he—

He’s a walking young-Millennial stereotype, is what I’m saying.

[Read: Leave James Bond alone]

He doesn’t appear old or tough or coldly professional enough to be Bond. Think of this: Connery was 31 when he filmed Dr. No and 32 in From Russia With Love. Moore was 44 in Live and Let Die. Dalton was 41 when he strapped on his Walther PPK. Craig was 37 when he sat at the card table in Casino Royale. Pattinson is 40—and yet all of these guys look self-assured and old enough to play Pattinson’s father, not his colleague. (Even Brosnan seems like a tougher old brother, not a fellow Double-O.)

Having most recently watched Pattinson mumble and anguish his way through The Batman, I cannot imagine him driving a Soviet tank through the streets of Russia, lecturing M on the finer points of blending cognac, or gently pushing the bad guy out of a space station’s airlock with an invitation to “take a giant step for mankind.” Perhaps the next film will do wonders; Moore, for one, was usually better when the scripts stuck to action instead of cheap comedy. But I have no faith, after the Craig psychodramas, that the writers will rescue Pattinson—or Bond.

Amazon MGM is trying hard to work up a new image for Pattinson. Their first look has him in a tux sighting a sniper rifle, his face half-shadowed and his hair (for once) combed. Maybe it’ll work. But I still cannot imagine him trading barbs with the likes of Goldfinger: I imagine that when the mad criminal offers him a mint julep, Pattinson will scowl and explain that alcohol and sugar are bad for you.

title: Are You Sure the Problem Is Pajamas, Sean Duffy?
summary: Well, well, well. If it isn’t my old nemesis, Sean Duffy, in the news again. Did something happen at the airports, Sean? Was it very bad? Would you go so far as to describe it as a serious problem? Worse, say, than people dressing casually at the airport, perhaps even in pajamas? Because I would.Yes...
content:
Well, well, well. If it isn’t my old nemesis, Sean Duffy, in the news again. Did something happen at the airports, Sean? Was it very bad? Would you go so far as to describe it as a serious problem? Worse, say, than people dressing casually at the airport, perhaps even in pajamas? Because I would.

Yes, it’s me, Pajamas.

Now, I’m only a breathable, comfortable nighttime garment, but I think it is good when the planes aren’t afraid to go up and then come down again. To me, that is the most important thing that happens at an airport. Call me old-fashioned, but I think the planes should get to leave the ground. That’s just a superstition I have!

A total ground stop. Planes everywhere, stuck on the tarmacs; spoonfuls of mashed bananas, unable to reach reluctant toddlers’ mouths. For hours, you say? Now, that sounds like a real airport problem. It would be a shame if you had alienated your old friend Travel Pajamas in a situation like this.

I do not mean to question how much you know about aviation. I am just a simple set of sleep garments. My job is to help people sleep easily. I don’t know what your job is! Something where you get to appear on television a lot and nothing is your fault?

In times of trouble, Mr. Rogers always told us to look for the helpers. Well, pajamas were there, helping. Pajamas swathed travel-weary limbs in a soft fabric embrace. Where were you? Saying on CNN that you “take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations”? That doesn’t sound like taking responsibility. But then again, I am just sleepwear. I am cozy with everyone, not just the industry I am meant to regulate.

The fact that your reality-TV show (no, not The Real World, the other one) was called The Great American Road Trip and not Touring America Safely via Uninterrupted Air Travel should perhaps have signaled to us that all was not well.

I know you love a scapegoat. I was your first. And now I am sure you will find someone to blame. Blame AI! Blame “systems”! Blame the “patriot” who installed the router! Say you don’t know what the problem was, but you will need $50 billion to fix it! That won’t fly, not unlike every plane on Friday night.

I would suggest that this incident was someone’s chickens coming home to roost—or they would have been coming home to roost if there weren’t a ground stop. This was a case of chickens circling above the airport hoping for permission to land, then being stuck on the tarmac for hours.

When you slandered me, all those months ago, and blamed me for everything that was wrong with air travel, I held my peace. I kept it buttoned. But now I am asking respectfully (I know respect means a lot to you) for my apology. Was the problem really that people were not dressing like it was 50 years ago, Sean? Was that really the problem?

Thank you for your time. Good day! I will see you this evening, when I will do my best to make you as happy and comfortable as you have failed to make me.

Sincerely,

Pajamas

content:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
